newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico's Mancera defends peso policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico's Mancera defends peso policy.

text.p: Banco de Mexico Governor Miguel Mancera on Thursday defended his policy of maintaining a free-floating peso, arguing that a permanently undervalued exchange rate may do as much harm as good.

At the end of a year of relative exchange-rate stability, in which he was criticised by some sectors when the peso's margin of undervaluation against the dollar shrank, the central bank chief stressed his prime duty was controlling inflation.
For instance, when the peso began a slide in October, Banco de Mexico left the money markets short of 20 million pesos to push up interest rates to stop the currency from fueling inflation.

"The Bank of Mexico made this decision because large and abrupt increases in the exchange rate bring about inflationary consequences that, in the end, make it more difficult to bring rates down," Mancera said.
In October, the peso slid from around 7.5 pesos per dollar to eight pesos. On Thursday, the benchmark 48-hour or spot contract closed at 7.9050/7.9080 per dollar.

Giving his reasons for the steep October peso drop, Mancera said uncertainty ahead of the signing of an economic recovery pact, problems with petrochemical and rail privatizations, and accumulated inflation differentials between the United States and Mexico played their parts.

But wheras some sectors, such as exporters, had argued that a steep peso drop was long overdue, Mancera indicated that he did not favor maintaining a permanently undervalued exchange rate to foster economic growth.
"Even though there are some groups that apparently benefit from a permanently undervalued exchange rate, there are also those who would suffer from such a situation," he said.

"It should be recalled that an ever undervalued exchange rate perpetuates the depression of real wages and the existence of high inflation and interest rates. This effects consumption, investment and, consequently, economic performance as a whole."
"The idea that a permanently undervalued exchange rate fosters economic growth, or that it is beneficial to all, is not persuasive," he said.
On the other hand, he said Banco de Mexico had not intervened this year to stop gradual depreciations brought on by market forces.

"It must also be emphasized that the current monetary and exchange-rate policies are in no way designed to forestall the depreciation of the domestic currency, should the fundamental conditions of the economy so warrant," he said.

Referring to the performance of the economy, he reiterated that it was expected to achieve at least four percent growth this year and next, noting that as well as export growth, "in 1996 it is already possible to recognize the positive contributions of consumption and investment."
Export momentum continued strong, he said, and year-end inflation was expected to be around half last year's level of 52 percent.
